title: The little rainbow fish
summary: A shy little fish finds friends at the bottom of the sea.

scenes.text: In the deepest part of the sea, much further down than the boats reach, where the water is blue, blue, and cool, swam a very special fish. He was tiny, the size of an apple, with a fan-shaped tail. But the most magical thing about him were his scales: they shone with all the colors of the rainbow at the same time. Red on his tail, orange on his belly, yellow on his back, green on his fins, blue on his neck, and violet on his head. When a sun ray came down to the bottom of the sea and hit a scale, the water all around filled up with sparkles. But — and this is the "but" of our story — the little fish was very, very shy. When other fish swam by, laughing or playing, he hid behind the corals and stayed very, very still, almost without breathing. He was afraid of speaking, afraid of playing, afraid they'd laugh at him. He spent his days alone, watching the slow rise of the bubbles. He counted them one by one: one, two, three, four, five. The ocean was his home, but also his hiding place.

One calm morning, the little fish was in his coral counting bubbles. Then a purple octopus with eight long arms arrived and stopped right in front of him. He was a friendly octopus, with two googly eyes and a crooked smile. "Hi, hi, hi!" he said waving all his tentacles at the same time. The little fish, scared, slipped further into the coral, almost trembling. "I want to play," he wanted to say. But the word got stuck. The octopus, without moving from where he was, waited very patiently. "I saw your colors from far away. They're so beautiful. They're like a rainbow in the water, did you know?" The little fish peeked out one eye from between the corals. The octopus wasn't coming any closer, wasn't insisting, just smiling at him. "Want to play with me? I know a really fun game," he offered, tilting his head. The little fish poked his whole head out, hesitated for a second, looked all around, and finally answered in a whisper: "Okay... but just a little bit."

The octopus taught him a hide-and-seek game among the green seaweed that swayed like dancers. "I count to ten and you hide," he explained. At first, the little fish played close to the coral, without going far, looking back every two seconds in case something scared him. But the octopus was such a terrible hider, so funny, that the little fish couldn't hold it anymore: the octopus would tuck himself behind a stone, but his eight arms would stick out from every side, like a flower with tentacles. And then, for the first time in his life, out of the little fish slipped a laugh. First it was a short sound, hee hee. Then a bigger one, ha ha ha. And finally an enormous burst of laughter that rose all the way to the surface, hahahaha!, loaded with colored bubbles. The little fish's scales shone so much that he looked like an underwater firework. For the first time in his life, he felt a soft warmth in his heart. The octopus laughed with him, contagious, and the two of them ended up rolling on the sandy floor of the sea.

The loud giggling and the bright colors attracted other neighbors from the bottom of the sea, curious. First a pink starfish appeared, with five points that moved like small fingers. "What's going on here that's so fun?" she asked. Then came a green seahorse, all elegant with his coiled tail. Then a yellow crab walking sideways, click, click, click. Then a silvery sardine and a small octopus who was the big octopus's son. Soon a group of friends had formed at the very bottom of the sea, all playing together among the corals. They played hide and seek, chase, who could make the most bubbles. The whole ocean filled up with laughter. The little rainbow fish wasn't alone anymore. His colors lit up the whole group, like a happy lantern. He learned three important things that morning: that his colors weren't for hiding, they were a gift to make others happy. That shyness goes away little by little, by playing. And that having a patient friend is the most beautiful thing in the world. From that day on, every time a new fish felt lonely or scared at the bottom of the sea, the little rainbow fish was the first to come over and say, with a smile: "Want to play with me?"
